name: Belshazzar
role: King in Babylon on the night it fell
whenBasis: The fall of Babylon to Cyrus, dated by the Nabonidus Chronicle to October 539 BC. Daniel's visions in chapters 7 and 8 are dated to his first and third years.
summary: King of Babylon who held a feast for a thousand nobles and drank from the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem, praising his gods. The fingers of a human hand wrote on the plaster of the wall. None of his wise men could read it; Daniel read MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN, and told him his kingdom was numbered, weighed and divided. That very night he was killed.
body: The queen reminds him of Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made chief of the wise men. Daniel refuses his gifts, recalls how Nebuchadnezzar was humbled until he acknowledged the Most High, and charges Belshazzar with knowing all this and not humbling his heart. Belshazzar still has him clothed in purple and proclaimed third ruler in the kingdom.

later.text: Babylonian texts name Belshazzar (Bel-šarra-uṣur) as the eldest son of the last king, Nabonidus, who left him in charge of Babylon for ten years while he stayed at Tema in Arabia. William Shea reads Daniel's “third ruler” in that light; Keil and Delitzsch and James Montgomery read the word as “one of three.” See the card on Belshazzar.

later.text: Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar his father. Nabonidus was not of Nebuchadnezzar's family, so Hartman and Di Lella see an error. Keil took Belshazzar for Nebuchadnezzar's own son and successor Evil-merodach (2 Kings 25:27), as did Hofmann, Hävernick, Hupfeld, Niebuhr and others he names; Ebrard and Franz Delitzsch, as Keil reports, took him for the later king Laborosoarchod. Albert Barnes and A. R. Fausset read “father” as grandfather, the Semitic use of the word reaching beyond the first degree. S. R. Driver allows that Nabonidus may have married a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, making him Belshazzar's grandfather on his mother's side, but notes that none of Nabonidus's inscriptions implies any relationship to Nebuchadnezzar.
